claims.quote: only on a very much larger, longer scale

claims.claim: Le Guin says prose rhythms are hard to talk about because we have no vocabulary for them.

claims.claim: Le Guin says reading aloud makes you aware of a word or phrase that tangles up the pace and needs to be moved or removed.

verdicts.trueWording: the planet was placed under Interdict by the Allworld HILF Authority
verdicts.note: Live site returned a 403 JS challenge; read via the Wayback raw capture 20260605103418id_. The line sits in the SECOND quoted handbook entry (the 'Number 62: FOMALHAUT II' block introduced by 'And a little later in the narrative'), under History, exactly where the claim points. All four limbs present in the one sentence: dated (a year opens the clause), passive voice, the imposing authority named, and a trailing 'pending...' clause giving the reason it stands.

verdicts.trueWording: cast in much more factual, sci fi style
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Sentence sits under the heading 'The plot' and contrasts the opening Semley story, told in 'olde worlde, fake folk tale style', with the rest of the narrative. Both limbs of the claim (folk-tale opening vs more factual rest) are in that one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: opening with his survey of “hominoid” species on the world
verdicts.note: Live page fetched raw (HTTP 200). Byline 'By Anand Pandian', dated January 26, 2018, anthrodendum. Quote is verbatim, curly quotes included, in the paragraph beginning 'Le Guin's mother, Theodora Kroeber...' which contains the line 'Le Guin's books teem with anthropologists'. The page names the subject an interplanetary ethnographer and completes the phrase with the specific world (Fomalhaut II); the claim's 'one world' is a fair generalisation, not an added limb.

verdicts.trueWording: everything is direct, concrete, and simple
verdicts.note: PDF fetched as binary and text-extracted with pdftotext (route 3). Title page reads 'Ursula K. Le Guin's "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)'. The sentence reads that Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking, he has no ichor, then the quoted clause; it sits in the paragraph on Tolkien's plain, clear English, on the eighth text page of the extraction (the claim's p.8 checks out). Scope note: the page's 'everything' covers Tolkien's prose generally rather than the vocabulary alone, which entails rather than contradicts the claim's narrower reading.

verdicts.trueWording: only on a very much larger, longer scale
verdicts.note: Live ursulakleguin.com page fetched raw (HTTP 200); answer to Alex, question 1. Quote verbatim. The 'than metrical feet' limb is carried by the immediately preceding sentence, which rules metric feet and verses out because this is prose, not poetry -- adjacent-sentence support, not a separate assertion.

verdicts.trueWording: we have no vocabulary for them
verdicts.note: Same page and answer. Full clause runs 'And they're hard to talk about, since we have no vocabulary for them', where 'they' is prose rhythms from the prior sentence. Both limbs (hard to talk about; no vocabulary) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I don’t think consciously about the rhythmic factors in a story
verdicts.note: Same page and answer. Sentence opens 'Whether I'm composing or re-writing,' then the quoted clause verbatim, curly apostrophe included. The composing/rewriting limb is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: a word or a phrase that tangles up the pace
verdicts.note: Same page and answer. Full sentence begins 'Reading aloud, you're aware of' the quoted phrase 'and needs to be moved or removed'. Both the reading-aloud limb and the moved-or-removed limb are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Wherever you hesitate in your reading aloud may reveal a fault
verdicts.note: Same page and answer; the sentence continues 'in the rhythm, the forward flow of the words', which supplies the claim's 'fault in the rhythm' limb. The context is explicitly reading your own prose aloud.

verdicts.trueWording: This general description implies very little
verdicts.note: Live ursulakleguin.com page fetched raw (HTTP 200), answer to Nicole and Bayla, the invented planet Teg / place Horb demonstration. The specimen sentence immediately before the quote places Horb on the coast of the southernmost of the nine continents of Teg, matching the claim word for word in substance. Horb is treated as a town/city later in the same answer (streets, ports, Palace gate, 'the city').

verdicts.trueWording: it has a long-established trading economy
verdicts.note: Same page and answer. The second specimen sentence (traders, windships, voor-pelts and diamonds) is followed by Le Guin's list of what 'we also learn', which includes the quoted clause verbatim. The 'without stating it' limb is supported by the framing question she is answering -- how much you can imply in a description.

verdicts.trueWording: packing your sentences with specifics, not with generalities
verdicts.note: Same page and answer. The paragraph after the two specimen sentences states that the difference is in specificity, then prescribes embodying it in concrete, vivid details, ending in the quoted phrase verbatim. Both limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: so long as your world looks and smells and tastes real
verdicts.note: Same page, final paragraph of the answer to Nicole and Bayla. Full sentence: you can fake quite a lot or leave it unsaid, then the quoted clause. Caveat recorded, not a downgrade: the page conjoins two further conditions after this one (complexity, emotional weight, integrity), which the claim omits; the claim asserts no exclusivity, so no limb is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: you have to describe more than a realist does
verdicts.note: Live publicbooks.org page fetched raw (HTTP 200); byline John Plotz, dated 6.15.2015, matching the claim's attribution. Quote verbatim in Le Guin's answer ('UL:') in section I, which opens 'I'm very strong on accuracy and exactitude' and continues that the leaving-out is half the art.

Live locusmag.com excerpts page fetched raw (HTTP 200); page headed 'Ursula K. Le Guin: A Return to Earthsea', September 2001, 'Excerpts from the interview'. The final excerpt contains 'In fact, I've learned to stop fiddling and twiddling' and, two sentences later, the quoted sentence verbatim. The claim's causal 'because' is carried by the intervening sentence on overpolished fiction being a bore, i.e. by Le Guin's juxtaposed rationale rather than by an explicit connective.
